## Investigación con agentes (Claude Opus 5.5; puede contener errores)
# Research notes: will the Supreme Court of India have at least 3 sitting women judges by 17 Oct 2026? (compiled 5 Oct 2026)

**Summary:** Two women sit on the Court today. The Collegium recommended Justice Sunita Agarwal on 28 Sep 2026, and her appointment would bring the count to three. As of about 5 Oct no government notification or oath had been found. No judge retires before the window.

## 1. What the resolution source shows
- **Official list:** https://www.sci.gov.in/chief-justice-judges/ returned HTTP 403 when fetched on 5 Oct 2026. Nothing below was read directly from it, so it remains unverified.
- **Count from secondary sources:** 34 sitting judges, 2 of them women:
  - B.V. Nagarathna, retires 29 Oct 2027
  - V. Mohana, sworn in 2 Jun 2026, retires 26 Jun 2031
  - Sources:
    - Wikipedia sitting-judges list, last edited 2 Oct 2026: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sitting_judges_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_India
    - SCC Online, 29 Sep 2026: "At present, the judges' strength of the Court is at 34 Judges against the sanctioned strength of 38 Judges." https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/09/29/sc-collegium-recommends-three-hc-chief-justices-as-judges-sc/
- **Sanctioned strength is now 38, not 34:**
  - Ordinance promulgated 16 May 2026.
  - Lok Sabha passed the replacement Bill on 3 Aug 2026.
  - Presidential assent on 11 Aug 2026 (date per Wikipedia; LawBeat reported the assent on 12 Aug).
  - Source: https://lawbeat.in/top-stories/president-assents-to-supreme-court-number-of-judges-amendment-act-2026-strength-increased-to-38-1621522
  - That leaves 4 vacancies, so there is room for all three nominees.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** this was not fetched. It is only relevant as a fallback that defines "credible sources".

## 2. Recent news and current status
- **28 Sep 2026 recommendation:** the Collegium led by CJI Surya Kant (with Vikram Nath, Nagarathna, Sundresh and Narasimha) recommended three High Court chief justices:
  - Sunita Agarwal, Chief Justice of Gujarat HC
  - D.K. Upadhyaya, Chief Justice of Delhi HC
  - Aparesh Kumar Singh, Chief Justice of Telangana HC
  - Sources:
    - The Leaflet, 28 Sep: https://theleaflet.in/supreme-court/supreme-court-collegium-recommends-three-high-court-chief-justices-none-in-line-to-be-cji
    - LiveLaw: https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/collegium-recommends-elevation-of-three-high-court-chief-justices-as-supreme-court-judges-552143
- **SC Observer (about 29 Sep, article undated):** "If the appointment of Justice Agarwal is notified, the Supreme Court will have three women judges… The Union is yet to notify their appointments." https://www.scobserver.in/journal/three-new-judges-recommended-for-the-supreme-court/
- **Business Standard (29 Sep):** headline "Number of women judges in Supreme Court likely to go up to three". Only the search snippet was seen; the page returned 403.
- **Notification status (searches around 5 Oct 2026):** no notification or swearing-in was found. Wikipedia lists Agarwal as "Nominee", with assumed office "TBC". This is uncertain: news indexing may lag by a day or two.
- **Possible friction (The Leaflet, 28 Sep):** Aparesh Kumar Singh was superseded in June 2026 and would now sit junior to Shree Chandrashekhar. No reports of government objections were found. The Centre could also notify the names separately, which has happened before, mostly with High Court appointments.
- **Agarwal's background:** born 30 Apr 1966, retires 29 Apr 2031, Gujarat HC Chief Justice since 23 Jul 2023. She is described as the only woman HC chief justice. In Aug 2025 there was criticism when Vipul Pancholi was elevated over her and other senior women judges.
- **No scheduled events that would reduce the count:**
  - No Supreme Court judge retires before 17 Oct 2026. The next retirement is S.C. Sharma on 29 Nov 2026.
  - CJI Surya Kant serves until 9 Feb 2027.
- **Prediction markets (checked 5 Oct 2026):**
  - Manifold: no relevant market. The only hits were unrelated, e.g. "Prediction markets legalized in India by 2035?" at about 157 mana volume.
  - Polymarket and Metaculus: nothing found, though this was not exhaustively verified.

## 3. Base rates and timing
- **Time from recommendation to swearing-in, recent Supreme Court batches:**

| Batch | Recommended | Notified | Sworn in | Days to oath |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aradhe, Pancholi | 25 Aug 2025 | 27 Aug | 29 Aug | 4 |
| Anjaria, Bishnoi, Chandurkar | ~26 May 2025 | — | ~30 May | ~4 |
| Mohana + 4 others | 22/27 May 2026 | ~31 May–1 Jun | 2 Jun | ~6–11 |
| Manmohan | 28 Nov 2024 | 3 Dec | 5 Dec | 7 |
| K.V. Chandran | 7 Jan 2025 | — | 16 Jan | 9 |
| N.K. Singh, Mahadevan | 11 Jul 2024 | — | 18 Jul | 7 |

  - Sources:
    - SCC Online, Aradhe/Pancholi oath (29 Aug 2025): https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2025/08/29/justice-alok-aradhe-justice-vipul-m-pancholi-take-oath-as-sc-judges/
    - SCC Online, Mohana batch appointed (1 Jun 2026): https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/06/01/president-appoints-4-chief-justices-and-v-mohana-as-supreme-court-judges/
    - SCC Online, Manmohan appointed (3 Dec 2024): https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2024/12/03/justice-manmohan-appointed-sc-judge-legal-news/
  - Some 2023–2025 dates came partly from a subagent's memory and may be off by 1–2 days.
- **Slow outliers:** Dipankar Datta took about 76 days (recommended 26 Sep 2022, sworn in 12 Dec 2022). The Dec 2022 batch of five took about 55 days (sworn in 6 Feb 2023). Both came during open friction between the Centre and the Collegium.
- **Agarwal's elapsed time:** about 7 days so far (as of 5 Oct). That is already slower than the 2–5 day notification lag of the latest batches, but within the range for batches since 2023. The window opens 15 Oct, about day 17, and closes 17 Oct, about day 19.
- **Periods with 3 or more women judges** (reconstructed from appointment dates; uncertain):
  - Aug 2018 to Jul 2020: 3 (Banumathi, Malhotra, Banerjee)
  - 31 Aug 2021 to 23 Sep 2022: 4, the all-time high
  - 23 Sep 2022 to 1 Sep 2024: 3
  - 1 Sep 2024: fell to 2
  - 9 Jun 2025: fell to 1 when Trivedi retired
  - 2 Jun 2026: rose to 2 with Mohana
  - Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_judges_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_India
- **Women appointed:** 12 women have ever served on the Court. Of about 31 appointments from 2022 to Sep 2026, only one was a woman (Mohana).

## Flags
- Everything in sections 1 and 2 happened before the question opened, including the 28 Sep recommendation. That is fine: resolution depends only on who is on the list between 15 and 17 Oct 2026.
- The official list could not be checked because of the 403 error.
- Agarwal's notification status after about 29 Sep is unconfirmed. It needs a re-check closer to the window.

criterios: This question resolves YES if the official "Chief Justice & Judges" list of sitting judges of the Supreme Court of India at https://www.sci.gov.in/chief-justice-judges/ shows at least three women among the sitting judges at any point between October 15, 2026 and October 17, 2026 (inclusive). It resolves NO otherwise. A judge counts as a sitting woman judge if she appears on that list (i.e., has been sworn in and has assumed office) and is a woman. As of October 1, 2026, the list shows two women judges: Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice V. Mohana. For example, if Justice Sunita Agarwal (or any other woman) is sworn in and appears on the list alongside these two, the count reaches three and the question resolves YES.
letra_pequena: A woman recommended by the Collegium but not yet sworn in (not appearing on the sitting-judges list) does not count. If the list at the primary URL is temporarily unavailable, the determination may be made from an equivalent official Supreme Court of India page or report from [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reflecting the composition of sitting judges during the window.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** From October 5, there are 10 days until the resolution window opens and 12 days until it closes on October 17.

(b) **Status quo:** NO. The Court currently has two sitting women judges, and a Collegium recommendation alone does not change that count.

(c) **Reference class:** In the eight appointment batches summarized by the research assistant, six reached the oath within roughly 11 days of recommendation; two took more than 50 days. That is a roughly **75% base rate for an oath by day 19**, though the small sample and the lack of a reported notification so far warrant caution.

(d) **NO scenario:** The government does not process Justice Agarwal’s recommendation soon enough, or she is not sworn in and listed by October 17.

(e) **YES scenario:** Her appointment is notified, she takes the oath, and the official sitting-judges list adds her alongside Justices Nagarathna and Mohana during October 15–17.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** The decisive event is **appearing as a sitting judge on the list during that three-day window**—not merely being recommended or having an appointment announced.

Probability: 78%

(a) As of October 5, there are 12 days until the October 17 deadline; the qualifying window begins in 10 days.

(b) If nothing changes, the Court has two sitting women judges, so the outcome is **No**.

(c) In the research assistant’s small sample, six of eight comparable appointment batches reached the oath within roughly 11 days of recommendation; two took more than 50 days. The recent pattern favors a timely appointment, though the absence of a confirmed notification after a week is a caution.

(d) **No:** The government does not complete Justice Agarwal’s appointment, or she does not take oath and appear on the sitting-judges list, in time.

(e) **Yes:** Her appointment is notified and she takes oath soon enough to appear on the list during October 15–17, alongside Justices Nagarathna and Mohana.

(f) The literal test is the **sitting-judges list during October 15–17**, not the Collegium recommendation or even the appointment notification. An earlier oath qualifies if she remains listed during that window.

Probability: 75%

**(a) Time left:** About 12 days. Today is Oct 5, 2026, and the window is Oct 15–17. That is days 17–19 after the Sep 28 recommendation.

**(b) Status quo:** Two women judges sit on the Court. Justice Agarwal has not been notified or sworn in as of about Oct 5. If nothing changes, the answer is NO.

**(c) Reference class:** Time from Collegium recommendation to oath for Supreme Court elevations, 2023–2026.
- Most batches took 3–13 days:
  - Bindal and Kumar: about 13 days.
  - Mishra and Viswanathan: 3 days.
  - Bhatti and Bhuyan: about 8 days.
  - Masih: 3 days.
  - Varale: about 6 days.
  - The 2024–2026 batches: 4–11 days.
- The outliers were 55 and 76 days, both in late 2022 during open friction between the Centre and the Collegium.
- Unconditionally, about 85–90% of elevations are sworn in by day 19.
- This one has already passed day 7 with no notification, which is slower than every recent batch. That points to some hold-up, so the conditional probability is lower, perhaps about 55–65%.

**(d) NO scenario:** The government sits on the file, for example over the supersession issue raised about Aparesh Kumar Singh, or simply out of administrative delay. Notification slips past mid-October, possibly into the Dussehra break around Oct 20 and the Diwali season. Agarwal is not on the list by Oct 17.

**(e) YES scenario:** The Centre notifies all three names, or segregates the batch and notifies Agarwal, in the week of Oct 5–14. She takes oath a day or two later, and the sitting-judges list shows three women by Oct 15–17.

**(f) Technicalities:**
- She must actually be sworn in and appear on the list, or in credible reports of the Court's composition, by Oct 17. Notification alone is not enough.
- An oath on Oct 15–17 itself still counts.
- No retirements before the window can reduce the count.
- The research may lag by a day or two, so a notification could already have happened without being picked up. That nudges the estimate slightly upward.

The delay so far is mildly worrying. Still, most Supreme Court elevations under this CJI's tenure have gone through quickly, and nothing reported suggests government objection to Agarwal herself.

Probability: 60%
